## Four chords, or four melodies?

Play C-F-G-C with every chord in root position. The harmonic route is perfectly
clear and the upper parts leap every time the root does. Now revoice the same
progression so common tones stay put and everything else travels by step. The
chords stop sounding like a sequence of objects and start sounding like four
lines going somewhere together.

*Voice leading* is the shaping of those lines. Store a four-part texture as
soprano, alto, tenor and bass arrays and each voice keeps its own history across
every chord boundary. Total movement makes a decent first objective. It's only a
first objective, though, and this lesson is mostly about what that number fails
to notice.

## Three renderings of one progression

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 72
use_synth :piano

define :play_lines do |lines, muted|
  lines.each do |name, pitches|
    next if name == muted
    in_thread do
      pitches.each do |pitch|
        play pitch, release: 1.6, amp: 0.55
        sleep 2
      end
    end
  end
  sleep 8
end

naive = {
  bass: [48, 53, 55, 48], tenor: [60, 65, 67, 60],
  alto: [64, 69, 71, 64], soprano: [67, 72, 74, 67]
}

led = {
  bass: [48, 53, 55, 48], tenor: [55, 57, 55, 55],
  alto: [60, 60, 59, 60], soprano: [64, 65, 62, 64]
}

repaired = {
  bass: [48, 53, 55, 48], tenor: [55, 57, 59, 55],
  alto: [60, 60, 62, 60], soprano: [64, 65, 67, 64]
}

define :movement do |lines|
  lines.values.sum do |pitches|
    pitches.each_cons(2).sum { |a, b| (a - b).abs }
  end
end

# A chord is legal only if the four voices ascend strictly: no crossings,
# and no two voices landing on the same pitch.
define :collisions do |lines|
  order = [:bass, :tenor, :alto, :soprano]
  bad = []
  lines[:bass].each_index do |index|
    chord = order.map { |name| lines[name][index] }
    unless chord.each_cons(2).all? { |lower, upper| upper > lower }
      bad << [index, chord]
    end
  end
  bad
end

[["naive", naive], ["led", led], ["repaired", repaired]].each do |name, lines|
  puts "#{name}: movement=#{movement(lines)} collisions=#{collisions(lines)}"
end

play_lines naive, nil
play_lines led, nil
play_lines repaired, nil
[:bass, :tenor, :alto, :soprano].each { |name| play_lines(repaired, name) }
```

All three renderings contain the same C, F, G and C harmonies over the same bass
line. The log prints 56 for `naive`, 26 for `led` and 32 for `repaired`. Which
of the three do you expect to prefer? Hold onto that guess; one of these numbers
is lying to you.

The muted passes at the end drop one voice at a time from `repaired`, which
makes the remaining three much easier to follow. No pitch or timing changes when
a voice disappears.

## Push on the result

1. In `led`, change the soprano's G-chord note from 62 to 74. That octave costs
   twelve extra points and pulls your ear straight to one conspicuous jump,
   though you haven't touched a single pitch class.

2. Swap the tenor and alto values on any one chord of `repaired`. The vertical
   harmony survives intact, the two lines cross, and `collisions` now prints the
   offending chord. Listen for the moment where the lines stop being traceable
   from one event to the next.

3. Mute each voice of `repaired` in turn and work out which chord loses a root,
   a third or a leading tone. Then decide which absence damages the cadence
   most. Distance travelled tells you nothing about which pitch was carrying the
   important job.

## The cheapest answer is a broken one

Look at `led` again, at the third chord. Bass is 55 and tenor is 55. Those are
the same note.

A cost function that adds up absolute pitch differences loves a unison, because
zero movement is the cheapest move available. The tenor sat on G3 in chord one,
found G3 still legal in chord three, and stayed. Total movement dropped to 26,
the lowest of the three. Meanwhile the texture quietly fell from four sounding
pitches to three, and the tenor line went missing from the middle of a lesson
about tracking four independent lines.

That's the surprise worth carrying out of this lesson: **a low movement score is
not the same thing as good voice leading**. The score measures one property. It
had no way to see the collapse, because a unison is invisible to a function that
only ever looks at one line at a time.

`collisions` is the smallest repair that helps. It rebuilds each vertical chord
from the four arrays and demands that the pitches ascend strictly, which rejects
crossings and unisons in one test. Run it against `led` and chord index 2 comes
back flagged. `repaired` moves the tenor up to B3 there and lifts alto and
soprano to keep the chord ascending, and it costs 32 instead of 26. Six extra
points buys you back a voice.

Now listen to `repaired` and hear what the constraint still missed. Between the
F chord and the G chord, every voice moves up by exactly two semitones. Bass and
alto travel in parallel fifths and bass and soprano in parallel octaves, which
is the same defect that made [Lesson 29](29-cadences-are-punctuation.qmd)'s cadences worth hand-voicing. Add one
constraint, satisfy it, and a different problem takes the vacancy. An optimiser
sees exactly what you taught it to see.

## What the cost function can and cannot reach

`movement` sums absolute pitch differences between consecutive notes in each
line. Lower means less travel in this controlled example. The number is a cost
function and not a theory of good writing, and a serious search wants more in
it: reject crossings and unisons, keep every voice inside a singable range,
preserve the required chord tones, refuse parallel perfect intervals, and
reward contrary motion at a cadence.

Storing lines first changes what your program can be asked. A chord list
describes the pitches present at one moment. A voice matrix also records where
each pitch came from and where it goes next. Transpose that matrix and the
vertical chord view comes back unharmed, so you lose nothing by keeping the
horizontal histories.

[Lesson 27](27-inversions-voicing.qmd)'s greedy search picked the cheapest next chord at each boundary and
never looked further ahead. A global search can weigh the whole progression
before committing. An easy local choice sometimes leaves no smooth route into a
later chord, and a slightly larger move now can lower the total. Four voices
over a bounded candidate set stay small enough for exhaustive enumeration, so
you can inspect that trade-off directly.

Common tones affect articulation too. Zero movement already lowers the score,
and holding a note through a boundary is not acoustically the same as striking
it twice at one pitch. This renderer reattacks every event and hides the
difference. A more faithful version would merge equal adjacent notes within a
line, letting one sustained tone bind the changing harmony around it.

## Search the whole progression

Generate every voicing of C-F-G-C that fits fixed bass, tenor, alto and soprano
ranges of your own choosing. Throw out any candidate that crosses voices, puts
two voices on one pitch, or drops a required chord tone. Score each complete
four-chord path by total movement, then play the cheapest path beside the
root-position baseline.

Print both totals and all four voice arrays from the winner. Print them even
when the number looks good, because a score you can't trace back to four
readable lines is a score you have no reason to trust. Then listen: the
arithmetic promises less motion, and only your ears can tell you whether less
motion made the progression smoother or just quieter.
